findings.description: IPv6 literal addresses in URLs (e.g., http://[::1]/image.png) are not properly validated. The URL parser returns hostnames with brackets (e.g., '[::1]'), but isIPv4() and isIPv6() both return false for bracketed addresses. This causes the code to fall through to DNS lookup which fails, accidentally blocking ALL IPv6 literals (both restricted and public) instead of properly validating them.

The IPv6 unique-local address check uses case-sensitive startsWith('fc') and startsWith('fd'). While Node's URL parser normalizes hostnames to lowercase, using case-insensitive comparison would be more robust defense-in-depth.

The isRestrictedAddress function splits IP on '.' to create a parts array for IPv4 range checks. For IPv6 addresses, this creates a single-element array, and parts[1] is undefined. The subsequent numeric comparisons (parts[1] >= 64) correctly evaluate to false, but the code structure is confusing and could be clarified.

The SSRF protection tests don't cover IPv6 literal addresses (with brackets). Tests should verify that http://[::1]/, http://[fe80::1]/, http://[fc00::1]/ are blocked, and http://[2001:db8::1]/ is allowed.

testing_summary: All 312 tests pass, typecheck clean, biome clean, fallow audit clean. The SSRF protection is functionally tested for IPv4 addresses and hostnames, but IPv6 literal address handling has a bug that causes false negatives for public IPv6 literals.
risk_rationale: The SSRF fix is largely correct and well-tested for IPv4/hostnames, but has a bug in IPv6 literal address handling that incorrectly blocks public IPv6 literals. This is a functional bug (false negative) rather than a security bypass, but should be fixed before merge. Other changes are solid improvements with good test coverage.
